schools.summary: Gill counts the lot as the second of the seven drawn at Shiloh; Calvin calls it a mark not of honour but of disgrace, Jacob's sentence of scattering executed, and draws from the surveyors' error that God sometimes leaves his servants to act like men lest they plume themselves on their clear-sightedness.

Clarke reads the arrangement as providence fulfilling Jacob's word literally on both Simeon and Levi; Wesley gives both causes at once, the threatened scattering and Judah's excessive portion, and adds that Simeon was the least of the tribes and so fittest to be lodged inside another.

Henry notes the order — after Judah, Joseph and Benjamin because Jacob had put Simeon under disgrace, yet before the younger sons — and that the tribe produced no judge or prophet; the surveyors had thought the land larger than it proved.

debates.question: Why was Simeon settled inside Judah?

sides.position: to fulfil Jacob's sentence of dispersion on Simeon and Levi
because a closer survey showed Judah's portion far exceeded its need
both together, the tribe being also the smallest

2.pericope_label: Simeon's towns, from Beersheba to Baalath-beer

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch judge Sheba omitted from the Chronicles list by a copyist's error, state flatly that thirteen does not tally with fourteen names, note that four of the towns had already stood in Judah's register, and rule out one site for Baalath-beer because Simeon's territory lay in the Negeb and cannot have reached north of Hebron.

Gill reads the opening pair as one name to save the total of thirteen, citing Kimchi and Ben Melech, and wonders whether Beth-lebaoth held a Canaanite temple dedicated to lions, as Leontopolis did in Egypt.
Clarke refers most of the names back to the Judah list and supplies their meanings — the well of the oath, the city of chariots, the house of lionesses, the well of the mistresses.

themes: a list that will not add up

schools.summary: Gill explains that this is why Simeon gets no border of its own, Judah's having already been described; Calvin praises Judah's moderation in not pleading God's authority for a surplus fixed by human judgement, and in welcoming brethren who would otherwise have had nothing.
Keil and Delitzsch keep the wording exact — Judah's part was too much for them, so Simeon's inheritance lay within it.
Henry draws the rule: errors must be excepted and a review admitted, and the abundance of some must supply the wants of others, for there may be equity where there is not law.

themes: a lot corrected after the fact

10.pericope_label: Zebulun's third lot, and the border traced westward from Sarid

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch place the inheritance above the plain of Jezreel and say it touched neither the Mediterranean nor the Jordan; Ellicott traces the southern line past Jokneam and notes that it does not reach the sea, Asher's territory interposing. Both are uncertain where Sarid stood.

Gill has the border going westward to the Mediterranean, fulfilling Jacob and Moses on Zebulun as a haven of ships; Calvin makes the fulfilment an argument about revelation itself — a landless exile assigned his son a maritime district, and the lot confirmed it as if God thundered twice from heaven.
Henry reads the tribe by what it would become — Nazareth, the mount of the transfiguration, and the shore where Christ preached and wrought miracles lay in this lot.
Wesley states the sea-to-sea reading in its strongest form: washed by the midland sea on the west and the sea of Tiberias on the east, trading ships on the one and fishing ships on the other.

debates.question: Did Zebulun's territory actually reach the sea?

sides.position: yes — the lot fulfilled Jacob's word that Zebulun should be a haven of ships
no — the boundary touched neither the Mediterranean nor the Jordan, Asher lying between

themes: Sarid, the point nobody can fix

12.pericope_label: Zebulun's line eastward and round to the valley of Jiphtah-el

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch identify Chisloth-tabor from Kimchi as the flanks of Tabor, place Daberath and Gath-hepher and Rimmon from surviving villages, mark Eth-kazin and Neah unknown, and show that one supposed place-name is really a participle meaning 'bounded off'; Ellicott renders the same clause as Remmon that stretcheth to Neah, and puts Hannathon at the north-east corner where Keil and Delitzsch put the north-west.
Gill marks the turn from Sarid eastward, identifies Gath-hepher as Jonah's birthplace where Jerome says his grave was shown, and admits he has no account of Hannathon beyond Jerome's bare mention.

debates.question: Which corner of Zebulun does the last verse describe?

sides.position: the north-west, since the preceding verse had pointed east
the north-east

themes: a line certain, its points argued
a word mistaken for a place

15.pericope_label: Zebulun's towns, and a total that exceeds its list

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch take the towns one by one and are candid about how little survives, confident only of Bethlehem; Ellicott refers Ibzan the judge to this Bethlehem rather than the southern one, notes the name occurs in no other tribe, and suggests that some unidentified names may not be town-names at all.

Clarke marks this Bethlehem as a different place from that in which our Lord was born; Wesley explains the surplus of names by towns that were not cities properly so called, or bordered the tribe without belonging to it.
Gill notes that of the first two names we read nowhere else, and glosses the closing formula as what was allotted and then divided according to the number of the families.

debates.question: Why does the list hold more names than the total of twelve?

sides.position: some were not cities, or belonged to bordering tribes
some of the unidentified names may not be names of towns at all

17.pericope_label: Issachar's fourth lot, and the plain of Jezreel

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch say only towns are given here, the boundaries being traceable from the surrounding tribes, and describe Jezreel as Ahab's summer residence on a mountain overlooking the plain that took its name; Ellicott finds policy in the placing of Issachar and Zebulun beside Judah's old camp-fellows, and follows it into the gospels.

Clarke finds it remarkable that the lot distinguished the two brothers exactly as the prophetic Jacob had, the younger named first, and sees God's influence as plainly in the lot as on the patriarch's mind; he fixes Jezreel by its neighbours and remembers Shunem as Elisha's lodging and the Philistine camp before Gilboa. Wesley explains that the tribe is given by cities rather than borders, which were its neighbours'.

Henry sketches the rectangle from Jordan to the great sea and runs through the tribe's roll of places — Kishon, Gilboa, Megiddo — so that a list of towns becomes a table of contents for the histories.

themes: a list of towns as a table of histories

19.pericope_label: Issachar's inland towns, most of them lost

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch place Haphraim and En-gannim, give up Sion, Kishion and Abez, decline Knobel's emendation of Anaharath because the Greek manuscript behind it has two names where the Hebrew has one, and refuse his identification of Remeth on the ground that the modern name arose from the village's fortified look and has nothing in common with the Hebrew; Ellicott offers little but modern names and map references.
Gill places Hapharaim from Jerome, can say of Rabbith only that Jerome names it, and identifies Remeth by cross-reference to the Levitical and Chronicles lists rather than by any site.

22.pericope_label: The border to Tabor and Jordan, and the count of sixteen

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch agree the town is meant, note that Chronicles gives it to Zebulun and that it stood on Zebulun's border, and allow both that it might be counted here to make up sixteen and that the number itself may simply be incorrect; Ellicott marks which of these towns matter in the later history.
Gill takes Tabor here for the city rather than the mountain, and quotes Polybius describing it on a hill rising like a breast, with an ascent of more than fifteen furlongs.
Clarke reads Beth-shemesh as the house of the sun and takes the recurrence of the name for proof that sun-worship had generally prevailed in the country.

debates.question: Is Tabor counted to Issachar or to Zebulun?

sides.position: reckoned here to Issachar, since the sixteen cannot otherwise be made up
it stood on Zebulun's border and Chronicles assigns it there, so the number may be wrong

24.pericope_label: Asher's fifth lot, from Acco south to Carmel

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch give Asher the coast from Carmel to the northern boundary and note the description starts in the middle at Acco; they identify Helkath with a Druse village, leave Beten and Achshaph unfound, and dismiss Knobel's sycamore etymology for Amad as an argument whose weakness needs no pointing out. Ellicott finds policy in the pairing of Asher with Naphtali, each parted from his own brother, favouring a united Israel.

Clarke reads Carmel as the vineyard of God, so fruitful it passed into a proverb, distinguishes it from Carmel in Judah, records the temple on it in Vespasian's time, and weighs the disputed founding of the order named after it; Wesley marks the same distinction and reads the fruitfulness as answering the prophecy over Asher.
Gill takes Helkath for the Hukok of the Levitical list, reports Masius placing it above Ptolemais, and notes the lot entitled the tribe to what follows.

27.pericope_label: Asher's line inland to Cabul, and north to great Zidon

schools.summary: Clarke explains 'on the left hand' as meaning north, since a man giving directions faces the sunrise, and insists this Cabul is not the paltry land Solomon gave Hiram, so the verse is no argument for a late date for the book; Wesley reads Israel's failure to possess Sidon as a providence, lest so good a port draw them into commerce and its vices.

Keil and Delitzsch trace the turn east to Beth-dagon and show the circuit closing, since Asher's eastern boundary met Zebulun's north-west corner at the valley of Jiphtah-el; on Ebron they weigh the twenty manuscripts reading Abdon and decline to settle it, noting Asher's towns are not all given here anyway.
Gill treats Hebron here as the Abdon of the Levitical list, distinguished from the far better-known Hebron of Judah.

debates.question: Is 'Ebron' a copyist's error for Abdon?

sides.position: yes — Abdon stands in the Levitical list and twenty manuscripts read it here
holders: many writers, as reported by Keil and Delitzsch

sides.position: possible but uncertain, since the reading may have come from that list and Abdon may simply be omitted

themes: two registers meeting at a ravine

29.pericope_label: Ramah, the strong city of Tyre, and the close of Asher's lot

schools.summary: Clarke rejects the rendering 'the strong city Tyre' as a departure from the Hebrew, argues from Homer's silence that Tyre was unknown in Joshua's day, and explains the word as meaning simply a rock or stronghold; he also counts nearly thirty cities where the text says twenty-two and explains the surplus as frontier towns. Wesley agrees the boundary reached Tyre exclusively, the city being no part of the land given.
Keil and Delitzsch place Ramah at a village with ancient sarcophagi south-east of Tyre, and take the fortified town to be mainland Tyre, the present Sur, not the island city.
Henry passes on Bishop Patrick's conjecture that this continental stronghold was not the later island Tyre, and that many Canaanites took shelter in it and in Sidon when Joshua invaded.
Gill distinguishes the Ramah of Asher from that of Naphtali, and closes the lot with Josephus on the fruitfulness of the country from Carmel over against Sidon.

sides.position: not the famous Tyre at all — the word means a stronghold, and Tyre was unknown so early
Tyre on the mainland, distinct from the later island city

32.pericope_label: Naphtali's sixth lot, and a southern border nobody can read

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch warn at the outset that the lines cannot be traced with certainty, and place the oak-forest of Zaanannim near Kedesh north-west of Lake Huleh; Ellicott puts nearly all the same places instead near the Sea of Galilee on its south-west side, and says of 'Judah upon Jordan' that nothing certain can be said.

Gill marks the northern coast running west to east and admits its first point cannot be placed; Calvin reads the tribe against Jacob's 'hind let loose', though a correction appended to his own text shows his geography wrong, since Judah and Naphtali lie at opposite ends of the land with five tribes between.

Clarke states the difficulty plainly — Naphtali did not border on Judah, several tribes lying between — reports that omitting Judah with the Greek would solve it though no manuscript supports the omission, and passes on Houbigant's emendation, 'by the banks of Jordan'; Wesley explains the direction the boundary is traced.
Henry puts Naphtali furthest north, bordering Lebanon, with Leshem at its utmost edge — whence the reckoning from Dan to Beersheba — and notes that Capernaum and Bethsaida stood within it.

debates.question: What is meant by 'to Judah upon Jordan'?

sides.position: the text is corrupt; read 'by the banks of Jordan'
omit Judah with the Greek, though no manuscript warrants it
nothing certain can be said

themes: a blessing read into a boundary

35.pericope_label: The fenced cities of Naphtali, and the close of the sixth lot

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch reject Knobel's site for Ziddim because it falls in Issachar, dismiss his Zer as a very doubtful combination, place Hammath by its hot springs near Tiberias, describe Ramah's olive plantations and excellent well while admitting it has no relics of antiquity, and refuse the joining of Migdal-el to the next name as resting on nothing but similarity of sound; Ellicott notes the word 'fenced' as marking a frontier protected by fortresses, and reports Conder's confidence about Hazor.
Clarke counts twenty-three cities where the text says nineteen and explains the excess by frontier towns of other tribes; Wesley notes that Chinnereth gave the lake of Gennesaret its name.

Gill passes on the Talmud's later name for Ziddim, the village of wheat, identifies Kedesh in Galilee as one of the cities of refuge which Jerome knew as Cidissus, and closes the lot with Josephus's sweep from Damascus to the fountains of Jordan.

themes: another total that will not balance

40.pericope_label: Dan's seventh lot, wedged between Judah, Ephraim and the Philistines

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch explain that the territory was assembled from towns given up by Judah and Ephraim to match the tribe's numbers, and add that of Zorah, Eshtaol and Ir-shemesh the Danites took no possession, Judah having given them to the Levites, while two more towns stayed in Canaanite hands; Ellicott presses the census figures behind the arrangement and follows it to Samson and David, and asks whether the shared towns mark the border or lie inside it.
Wesley gives the same reason for the missing boundaries, Dan's borders being in part Judah's; Clarke glosses Ir-shemesh as the city of the sun, another proof of Canaanite idolatry.

Henry notes that Dan commanded the rear of the camp yet was provided for last, and reads the southern position as providence placing a numerous and powerful tribe in a post of danger against the Philistines — as it proved in Samson.
Gill notes the lot was the last drawn and that the tribe is described by its cities, several taken out of Judah, rather than by borders.

themes: a territory made from other tribes' towns

43.pericope_label: Dan's towns down to the territory before Japho

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch trace the obscure names through the later histories — Gibbethon in Philistine hands under the earliest kings, Baalath fortified by Solomon — place Jehud and Bene-berak in surviving villages, and infer from 'the territory before Japho' that Joppa itself did not belong to Dan, although the song of Deborah assumes the Danites held it.
Gill's refrain is that of these places we read nowhere else; he identifies Shaalabbin with the Shaalbim of Judges from Jerome, and Eltekeh as a Levitical city.

Clarke supplies the meanings and the later fame — Shaalabbin the foxes, kept constantly by the Amorites; Ekron a metropolis of one of the five Philistine dynasties; Japho the chief seaport in the possession of the twelve tribes.

sides.position: apparently not — the register stops at the territory before Japho
the Danites must have possessed it, by the song of Deborah

themes: a boundary stopping short of a port

47.pericope_label: Dan takes Leshem and calls it Dan, after Joshua's death

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch give the sequence without judgement — the Danites of Zorah and Eshtaol took Leshem after Joshua's death because their allotment was too small, being unable to drive the Amorites out — and identify the place with the mound at the central source of the Jordan; Ellicott reads the clause literally as territory lost rather than too little, and judges the Danites severely for preferring an easy conquest of a quiet people to the race set before them.

Clarke concedes the sense of the added words but reports Houbigant's conjecture of a copyist's slip, grants that the whole account describes what happened only after Joshua's death and calls it a later explicative note, and fixes Leshem at the northern extremity, whence the phrase from Dan to Beersheba; Wesley explains the notice as inserted so that all the Danites' chief places might stand together, and defends the migration as forced on them by bad neighbours.
Gill offers both readings of the clause and inclines to the literal one, that they lost part of their portion, being driven from the valley into the mountain by the Amorites.

debates.question: Did Dan's coast go out 'too little for them' or 'from them'?

sides.position: too little — the tribe outgrew its allotment
from them — the territory was lost to enemies, the added words being no part of the Hebrew

outliers.note: treats the whole paragraph as a marginal or explicative note added by a later hand, since it records events after Joshua's death.

49.pericope_label: Joshua's own inheritance, and the close of the division

schools.summary: Gill names the commissioners and allows two senses for that phrase, the Urim or an earlier word to Moses; Calvin praises the delay as proof of moderation, describes the requested city as a mere heap of stones chosen to make the grant less invidious, and answers the objection that Joshua should have served for nothing.

Wesley explains that Joshua could take nothing except by the people's gift, since the land was held by trustees, and glosses 'built' as repaired and enlarged; Clarke reports Timnath-serah as a barren spot in a barren country, and closes on the lot cast before the LORD, which left no room for murmuring.
Keil and Delitzsch reject any oracle through the high priest and refer the phrase to a promise given at Kadesh alongside Caleb's, unrecorded in the books of Moses.

Henry makes Joshua's being served last an example to all in public place, notes that he took his portion in his own tribe rather than distinguishing himself elsewhere and near the tabernacle, and reads 'according to the word of the LORD' as a special promise that made the portion doubly pleasant.

debates.question: What does 'according to the word of the LORD' refer to?

sides.position: an oracle by Urim and Thummim, or else an earlier word to Moses
not an oracle at all, but a promise given at Kadesh with Caleb's and not recorded in the Pentateuch
